method: Each claim checked against the retrieved text of the MJA overview of the Australian Guidelines for the Treatment of Alcohol Problems (2021). Evidence levels (A-D, GPP) transcribed exactly as the source attaches them. Doses are reported only where the source states them (thiamine; the 5-day diazepam limit); the oral diazepam regimen in Box 4 and the pharmacotherapy doses were not retrieved and are recorded as input_unavailable. The grading scheme's own definitions were not in the retrieved text and are not asserted.

claims.claim: The Guidelines for the Treatment of Alcohol Problems were released in April 2021, commissioned by the Commonwealth of Australia to remain current and integrated with the updated NHMRC Australian Guidelines to Reduce Health Risks from Drinking Alcohol, and have been periodically updated over the past 25 years
claims.source_text: Having been periodically updated over the past 25 years, the present version of the guidelines, released in April 2021, was commissioned by the Commonwealth of Australia to remain current and integrated with the updated National Health and Medical Research Council Australian Guidelines to Reduce Health Risks from Drinking Alcohol

claims.claim: People who experience alcohol-related problems often experience stigma, as these are frequently viewed as personal moral failings that are undeserving of sympathy
claims.source_text: People who experience alcohol-related problems often experience stigma, as these are frequently viewed as personal moral failings that are undeserving of sympathy.

claims.claim: Stigma is common across health care settings and is a significant barrier to accessing health and other services, with research finding examples of clinicians denying appropriate care such as regarding patients as less deserving of liver transplants
claims.source_text: Stigma is, unfortunately, common across health care settings for people experiencing problems with alcohol and it is a significant barrier to accessing health and other services. Research has found examples of clinicians denying appropriate care to patients experiencing problems (eg, regarding them as less deserving of liver transplants).

claims.claim: Patients have reported being offered advice based on clinicians' own opinions rather than evidence, and being talked down to, scolded and blamed for the problems they are experiencing with alcohol, and such experiences deter future and further help-seeking
claims.source_text: Patients have reported being offered advice based on clinicians' own opinions rather than evidence, and being talked down to, scolded and blamed for the problems they are experiencing with alcohol; such experiences deter future and further help-seeking.

claims.claim: Steps individual clinicians can take include using person-centred practice that treats patients with respect and compassion and includes the patient in decision making, using language consistent with guides produced by peer support organisations, and taking part in anti-stigma training especially training that is peer-led or has had substantial peer input
claims.source_text: use person-centred practice that treats patients with respect and compassion and includes the patient in decision making about their treatment; use language consistent with guides produced by peer support organisations, to prevent the use of any potential prejudicial or stigmatising language when communicating with patients and the general community; and take part in anti-stigma training, especially training that is peer-led or has had substantial peer input into its development.

claims.claim: Stigma should be addressed at the structural and organisational level as individual clinicians can struggle to make behavioural changes where this is not supported by the broader workplace
claims.source_text: Although stigma should be addressed at the structural and organisational level (as individual clinicians can struggle to make behavioural changes where this is not supported by the broader workplace)

claims.claim: Patients should be advised that alcohol use has no beneficial health effects, there is no clear risk-free threshold for alcohol intake, and the safe dose depends on factors such as underlying liver disease, comorbidities, age and sex (Level A)
claims.source_text: Patients should be advised that alcohol use has no beneficial health effects. There is no clear risk-free threshold for alcohol intake. The safe dose for alcohol intake is dependent on many factors such as underlying liver disease, comorbidities, age and sex (Level A).

claims.claim: The supplement does not recommend consuming alcohol for health benefits because the latest research indicates there are no net health benefits from alcohol use, there is a clear link between alcohol use and harm, and there is a risk that a non-drinker will develop an alcohol use disorder if drinking is recommended
claims.source_text: This supplement will also not recommend consuming alcohol for health benefits, because: (i) the latest research indicates there are no net health benefits from alcohol use; (ii) there is a clear link between alcohol use and harm; and (iii) there is a risk that a non-drinker will develop an alcohol use disorder if we recommend drinking alcohol.

claims.claim: The NHMRC guideline for adults is that to reduce the risk of harm from alcohol-related disease or injury healthy men and women should drink no more than 10 standard drinks a week and no more than 4 standard drinks on any one day, and the less you drink the lower your risk of harm
claims.source_text: To reduce the risk of harm from alcohol-related disease or injury, healthy men and women should drink no more than 10 standard drinks a week and no more than 4 standard drinks on any one day. The less you drink, the lower your risk of harm from alcohol.

claims.claim: The NHMRC guideline states that children and people under 18 years of age should not drink alcohol, that women who are pregnant or planning a pregnancy should not drink alcohol, and that for women who are breastfeeding not drinking alcohol is safest for their baby
claims.source_text: To reduce the risk of injury and other harms to health, children and people under 18 years of age should not drink alcohol. ... To prevent harm from alcohol to their unborn child, women who are pregnant or planning a pregnancy should not drink alcohol. For women who are breastfeeding, not drinking alcohol is safest for their baby.

claims.claim: There were 5552 deaths attributed to alcohol in 2017
claims.source_text: Alcohol-related deaths: these have risen, with 5552 deaths attributed to alcohol in 2017.

claims.claim: Alcohol consumption is linked to over 200 diseases including alcohol-related injuries, cancers, cardiovascular diseases and liver disease, contributing to 4.6% of Australia's overall burden of disease
claims.source_text: The link between alcohol and disease: alcohol consumption is linked to over 200 diseases, including alcohol-related injuries, cancers, cardiovascular diseases, and liver disease. This contributes to 4.6% of Australia's overall burden of disease.

claims.claim: In 2012-13 there were about 150 000 alcohol-related hospitalisations, and despite declines in consumption alcohol attributable emergency department presentations, hospitalisations and ambulance attendances have remained stable or increased
claims.source_text: in 2012-13, there were about 150 000 alcohol-related hospitalisations. Despite declines in consumption, alcohol attributable emergency department presentations, hospitalisations and ambulance attendances have remained stable or increased.

claims.claim: Conservative estimates in 2010 suggest a $14.4 billion cost to the economy, more than double Australia's alcohol-related tax revenue
claims.source_text: Conservative estimates in 2010 suggest a $14.4 billion cost to the economy, more than double Australia's alcohol-related tax revenue.

claims.claim: In 2017 per capita alcohol consumption in Australia was at its lowest within the past 50 years at 9.5 litres of pure alcohol consumed annually, yet alcohol is the sixth highest risk factor contributing to the burden of disease in Australia
claims.source_text: In 2017, per capita alcohol consumption in Australia was at its lowest within the past 50 years, at 9.5 L of pure alcohol consumed annually, yet it is the sixth highest risk factor contributing to the burden of disease in Australia.

claims.claim: Screening for unhealthy alcohol use and appropriate interventions should be implemented in general practice (Level A), hospitals (Level B), emergency departments and community health and welfare settings (Level C)
claims.source_text: Screening for unhealthy alcohol use and appropriate interventions should be implemented in general practice (Level A), hospitals (Level B), emergency departments and community health and welfare settings (Level C).

claims.claim: The Alcohol Use Disorders Identification Test is the most effective screening tool and is recommended for use in primary care and hospital settings, and for screening in the general community the AUDIT-C is a suitable alternative (Level A)
claims.source_text: The Alcohol Use Disorders Identification Test (AUDIT) is the most effective screening tool and is recommended for use in primary care and hospital settings. For screening in the general community, the AUDIT-C is a suitable alternative (Level A).

claims.claim: Quantity-frequency measures can detect consumption that exceeds levels in the current Australian guidelines (Level B)
claims.source_text: Quantity-frequency measures can detect consumption that exceeds levels in the current Australian guidelines (Level B).

claims.claim: Indirect biological markers should be used as an adjunct to screening (Level A), and direct measures of alcohol in breath and/or blood can be useful markers of recent use (Level B)
claims.source_text: Indirect biological markers should be used as an adjunct to screening (Level A), and direct measures of alcohol in breath and/or blood can be useful markers of recent use (Level B).

claims.claim: Assessment should include evaluation of alcohol use and its effects, physical examination, clinical investigations and collateral history taking (Level C), and assessment for alcohol-related physical problems, mental health problems and social support should be undertaken routinely (GPP)
claims.source_text: Assessment should include evaluation of alcohol use and its effects, physical examination, clinical investigations and collateral history taking (Level C). Assessment for alcohol-related physical problems, mental health problems and social support should be undertaken routinely (GPP).

claims.claim: Where there are concerns regarding the safety of the patient or others specialist consultation is recommended (Level C), and assessment should lead to a clear, mutually acceptable treatment plan which specifies interventions to meet the patient's needs (Level D)
claims.source_text: Where there are concerns regarding the safety of the patient or others, specialist consultation is recommended (Level C). Assessment should lead to a clear, mutually acceptable treatment plan which specifies interventions to meet the patient's needs (Level D).

claims.claim: Sustained abstinence is the optimal outcome for most patients with alcohol dependence (Level C)
claims.source_text: Sustained abstinence is the optimal outcome for most patients with alcohol dependence (Level C).

claims.claim: Risk factors for alcohol withdrawal include regular daily consumption of more than 80 grams of alcohol per day, previous withdrawal, and intercurrent illness including cessation of other drugs
claims.source_text: Risk factors include regular daily consumption of more than 80 grams of alcohol per day, previous withdrawal, and intercurrent illness including cessation of other drugs.

claims.claim: Withdrawal symptoms generally start 6-24 hours after the last drink, peak at 24-48 hours and subside within 2-4 days but may last a week, while cravings, mood changes and sleep disturbances may persist for several weeks
claims.source_text: withdrawal symptoms generally start 6-24 hours after the last drink, peak at 24-48 hours and subside within 2-4 days, but may last a week; cravings, mood changes and sleep disturbances may persist for several weeks.

claims.claim: Alcohol withdrawal symptoms range from trivial to severe life-threatening complications such as seizures and delirium, however mortality is low with good clinical care
claims.source_text: Alcohol withdrawal symptoms range from trivial to severe life-threatening complications (eg, seizures and delirium). However, mortality is low with good clinical care.

claims.claim: Most cases of withdrawal can be managed in an ambulatory setting with appropriate support (Level B), and tapering diazepam regimens (Level A) with daily staged supply from a pharmacy or clinic are recommended (GPP)
claims.source_text: Most cases of withdrawal can be managed in an ambulatory setting with appropriate support (Level B). Tapering diazepam regimens (Level A) with daily staged supply from a pharmacy or clinic are recommended (GPP).

claims.claim: Benzodiazepines are the preferred medication for alcohol withdrawal, supported by Level A evidence
claims.source_text: Benzodiazepines are the preferred medication, supported by Level A evidence

claims.claim: Diazepam access should be managed with daily pickup from a pharmacy or clinic or supervised by a responsible adult, diazepam use should be limited to a duration of 5 days, and if the patient continues to drink or is sedated doses should be withheld
claims.source_text: Diazepam access should be managed with daily pickup from a pharmacy or clinic, or supervised by a responsible adult, and diazepam use should be limited to a duration of 5 days. If the patient continues to drink or is sedated, doses should be withheld.

claims.claim: Medications for symptom management can be administered as required such as paracetamol, metoclopramide, hyoscine and loperamide
claims.source_text: Medications for symptom management can be administered as required (eg, paracetamol, metoclopramide, hyoscine and loperamide).

claims.claim: Withdrawal history taking should cover motivation and a realistic plan for abstinence with other treatment options considered if absent, alcohol and other drug use including quantity, frequency, duration and time of last use, previous withdrawal attempts and complications such as seizures, delirium and hallucinations, home environment and social supports, and medical and psychiatric conditions
claims.source_text: History taking should cover: motivation and a realistic plan for abstinence; if not, other treatment options should be considered; alcohol and other drug use, including quantity, frequency, duration, time of last use, and features of use disorder; previous withdrawal attempts and any complications (seizures, delirium and hallucinations); home environment and social supports; and medical and psychiatric conditions.

claims.claim: Examination before withdrawal should include vital signs, hydration, mental state, evidence of intoxication, withdrawal signs such as tremor, anxiety, sweating and tachycardia, and signs of liver disease and other complications
claims.source_text: Examination should include: vital signs (blood pressure, pulse rate and body temperature), hydration, mental state, evidence of intoxication, withdrawal signs (tremor, anxiety, sweating and tachycardia); signs of liver disease and other complications

claims.claim: Support during withdrawal should focus on strategies for coping with withdrawal symptoms, maintaining motivation and reassurance daily if possible, and linking the patient to a 24-hour telephone counselling service or crisis telephone service
claims.source_text: should focus on strategies for coping with withdrawal symptoms, maintaining motivation and reassurance (daily if possible). Linking the patient to a 24-hour telephone counselling service or crisis telephone service can also be of value.

claims.claim: Nutrition advice should include drinking at least 2 litres of fluid per day and avoiding heavy meals, and thiamine supplements of 300 mg per day for 7 days should be provided orally if the patient is well or by intramuscular injection if nutritionally depleted
claims.source_text: Nutrition advice should include drinking plenty of fluids (2 litres per day minimum) and avoiding heavy meals. Thiamine supplements (300 mg per day for 7 days) should be provided orally if the patient is well or by intramuscular injection if they are nutritionally depleted.

claims.claim: For suspected Wernicke encephalopathy higher thiamine doses are recommended initially, 500 mg total dissolved solids by intravenous infusion, with ongoing treatment guided by specialist advice
claims.source_text: For suspected Wernicke encephalopathy, higher thiamine doses are recommended initially (500 mg total dissolved solids by intravenous infusion) with ongoing treatment guided by specialist advice

claims.claim: Acamprosate is recommended to help maintain abstinence from alcohol (Level A) and naltrexone is recommended for prevention of relapse to heavy drinking (Level A)
claims.source_text: Acamprosate is recommended to help maintain abstinence from alcohol (Level A). Naltrexone is recommended for prevention of relapse to heavy drinking (Level A).

claims.claim: Disulfiram is only recommended in close supervision settings where patients are motivated for abstinence (Level A)
claims.source_text: Disulfiram is only recommended in close supervision settings where patients are motivated for abstinence (Level A).

claims.claim: Some evidence for the off-label therapies baclofen and topiramate exists but their side effect profiles are complex and neither should be a first-line medication (Level B)
claims.source_text: Some evidence for off-label therapies baclofen and topiramate exists, but their side effect profiles are complex and neither should be a first-line medication (Level B).

claims.claim: Cognitive behaviour therapy should be a first-line psychosocial intervention for alcohol dependence, and its clinical benefit is enhanced when combined with pharmacotherapy for alcohol dependence or an additional psychosocial intervention such as motivational interviewing (Level A)
claims.source_text: Cognitive behaviour therapy should be a first-line psychosocial intervention for alcohol dependence. Its clinical benefit is enhanced when it is combined with pharmacotherapy for alcohol dependence or an additional psychosocial intervention (eg, motivational interviewing) (Level A).

claims.claim: Motivational interviewing is effective in the short term and in patients with less severe alcohol dependence (Level A)
claims.source_text: Motivational interviewing is effective in the short term and in patients with less severe alcohol dependence (Level A).

claims.claim: Brief motivational interviewing interventions are more effective than no treatment for people who consume alcohol at risky levels (Level A), their effectiveness compared with standard care or alternative psychosocial interventions varies by treatment setting, and they are most effective in primary care settings (Level A)
claims.source_text: Brief motivational interviewing interventions are more effective than no treatment for people who consume alcohol at risky levels (Level A). Their effectiveness compared with standard care or alternative psychosocial interventions varies by treatment setting. They are most effective in primary care settings (Level A).

claims.claim: Residential rehabilitation may be of benefit to patients who have moderate-to-severe alcohol dependence and require a structured residential treatment setting (Level D)
claims.source_text: Residential rehabilitation may be of benefit to patients who have moderate-to-severe alcohol dependence and require a structured residential treatment setting (Level D).

claims.claim: Peer-led support programs such as Alcoholics Anonymous and SMART Recovery are effective at maintaining abstinence or reductions in drinking (Level A)
claims.source_text: Peer-led support programs such as Alcoholics Anonymous and SMART Recovery are effective at maintaining abstinence or reductions in drinking (Level A).

claims.claim: Return to problematic drinking is common and aftercare should focus on addressing factors that contribute to relapse (GPP), and a harm-minimisation approach should be considered for patients who are unable to reduce their drinking (GPP)
claims.source_text: Return to problematic drinking is common and aftercare should focus on addressing factors that contribute to relapse (GPP). A harm-minimisation approach should be considered for patients who are unable to reduce their drinking (GPP).

claims.claim: Active alcohol use disorder including dependence significantly increases the risk of overdose associated with the administration of opioid drugs, and specialist advice is recommended before treatment of people dependent on both alcohol and opioid drugs (GPP)
claims.source_text: Active alcohol use disorder, including dependence, significantly increases the risk of overdose associated with the administration of opioid drugs. Specialist advice is recommended before treatment of people dependent on both alcohol and opioid drugs (GPP).

claims.claim: Older patients requiring management of alcohol withdrawal should have their use of pharmaceutical medications reviewed given the prevalence of polypharmacy in this age group (GPP)
claims.source_text: Older patients requiring management of alcohol withdrawal should have their use of pharmaceutical medications reviewed, given the prevalence of polypharmacy in this age group (GPP).

claims.claim: Smoking cessation can be undertaken in patients with alcohol dependence and/or polydrug use problems, and some evidence suggests varenicline may help support reduction of both tobacco and alcohol consumption (Level C)
claims.source_text: Smoking cessation can be undertaken in patients with alcohol dependence and/or polydrug use problems; some evidence suggests varenicline may help support reduction of both tobacco and alcohol consumption (Level C).

claims.claim: More intensive interventions are needed for people with comorbid conditions as this population tends to have more severe problems and carries a worse prognosis than those with single pathology (GPP)
claims.source_text: More intensive interventions are needed for people with comorbid conditions, as this population tends to have more severe problems and carries a worse prognosis than those with single pathology (GPP).

claims.claim: The Kessler Psychological Distress Scale K10 or K6 is recommended for screening for comorbid mental disorders in people presenting for alcohol use disorders (Level A), and people with alcohol use disorder and comorbid mental disorders should be offered treatment for both disorders with care taken to coordinate intervention (Level C)
claims.source_text: The Kessler Psychological Distress Scale (K10 or K6) is recommended for screening for comorbid mental disorders in people presenting for alcohol use disorders (Level A). People with alcohol use disorder and comorbid mental disorders should be offered treatment for both disorders; care should be taken to coordinate intervention (Level C).

claims.claim: In patients with alcohol use disorder early recognition of the risk for liver cirrhosis is critical, patients with cirrhosis should abstain from alcohol and should be offered referral to a hepatologist for liver disease management and to an addiction physician for management of alcohol use disorder (Level A)
claims.source_text: In patients with alcohol use disorder, early recognition of the risk for liver cirrhosis is critical. Patients with cirrhosis should abstain from alcohol and should be offered referral to a hepatologist for liver disease management and to an addiction physician for management of alcohol use disorder (Level A).

claims.claim: Alcohol abstinence reduces the risk of cancer and improves outcomes after a diagnosis of cancer (Level A)
claims.source_text: Alcohol abstinence reduces the risk of cancer and improves outcomes after a diagnosis of cancer (Level A).

claims.claim: For patients with alcohol use disorder clinicians should have a high index of suspicion for cardiovascular diseases such as hypertension and dysrhythmia including supraventricular tachycardia and atrial fibrillation, these disorders increase stroke risk, and an abstinence-focused treatment plan is recommended for patients with cardiac disease to improve clinical outcomes
claims.source_text: For patients with AUD, clinicians should have a high index of suspicion for cardiovascular diseases such as hypertension and dysrhythmia (supraventricular tachycardia and atrial fibrillation). These disorders increase stroke risk. An abstinence-focused treatment plan for alcohol is recommended for patients with cardiac disease to improve clinical outcomes.

claims.claim: Wernicke encephalopathy, cerebellar dysfunction, subdural haematoma and alcohol-related dementia should be considered as differential diagnoses in patients with altered level of consciousness, falls, cognitive or motor decline, memory loss and alcohol use disorder
claims.source_text: Wernicke encephalopathy, cerebellar dysfunction, subdural haematoma, and alcohol-related dementia should be considered as differential diagnoses in patients with altered level of consciousness, falls, cognitive or motor decline, memory loss and AUD.

claims.claim: Alcohol abstinence, analgesia, a balanced diet, high dose thiamine and a multivitamin supplement containing other B vitamins are recommended for people with alcohol-related neurological disorders
claims.source_text: Alcohol abstinence, analgesia, a balanced diet, high dose thiamine and a multivitamin supplement containing other B vitamins are recommended for people with alcohol-re

claims.claim: Clinicians should screen women and men for domestic abuse (Level C), consider child protection assessments for caregivers with alcohol use disorder (GPP), and explore contraceptive options with women of reproductive age who regularly consume alcohol (Level B)
claims.source_text: Screen women and men for domestic abuse (Level C). Consider child protection assessments for caregivers with alcohol use disorder (GPP). Explore contraceptive options with women of reproductive age who regularly consume alcohol (Level B).

claims.claim: Pregnant and breastfeeding women should be advised that there is no safe level of alcohol consumption (Level B), and pregnant women who are alcohol dependent should be admitted to hospital for treatment in an appropriate maternity unit that has an addiction specialist (GPP)
claims.source_text: Advise pregnant and breastfeeding women that there is no safe level of alcohol consumption (Level B). Pregnant women who are alcohol dependent should be admitted to hospital for treatment in an appropriate maternity unit that has an addiction specialist (GPP).

claims.claim: A comprehensive HEEADSSS assessment should be performed for young people with alcohol problems (Level B), and treatment should focus on tangible benefits of reducing drinking through psychotherapy and engagement of family and peer networks (Level B)
claims.source_text: Perform a comprehensive HEEADSSS assessment for young people with alcohol problems (Level B). Treatment should focus on tangible benefits of reducing drinking through psychotherapy and engagement of family and peer networks (Level B).

claims.claim: Clinicians should collaborate with Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander health workers, organisations and communities and seek guidance on patient engagement approaches (GPP), and use validated screening tools and consider integrated mainstream and Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander-specific approaches to care (Level B)
claims.source_text: Collaborate with Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander health workers, organisations and communities, and seek guidance on patient engagement approaches (GPP). Use validated screening tools and consider integrated mainstream and Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander-specific approaches to care (Level B).

claims.claim: For culturally and linguistically diverse groups an appropriate method such as the teach-back technique should be used to assess the need for language and health literacy support (Level C), and engaging with culture-specific agencies can improve treatment access and success (Level C)
claims.source_text: Use an appropriate method, such as the “teach-back” technique, to assess the need for language and health literacy support (Level C). Engage with culture-specific agencies as this can improve treatment access and success (Level C).

claims.claim: Sexually diverse and gender diverse populations experience lower levels of satisfaction, connection and treatment completion (Level C) and clinicians should seek to incorporate LGBTQ-specific treatment and agencies (Level C)
claims.source_text: Be mindful that sexually diverse and gender diverse populations experience lower levels of satisfaction, connection and treatment completion (Level C). Seek to incorporate LGBTQ-specific treatment and agencies (Level C).

claims.claim: All new patients aged over 50 years should be screened for harmful alcohol use (Level D), alcohol should be considered as a possible cause for older patients presenting with unexplained physical or psychological symptoms (Level D), and shorter acting benzodiazepines should be considered for withdrawal management in older people (Level D)
claims.source_text: All new patients aged over 50 years should be screened for harmful alcohol use (Level D). Consider alcohol as a possible cause for older patients presenting with unexplained physical or psychological symptoms (Level D). Consider shorter acting benzodiazepines for withdrawal management (Level D).

claims.claim: Cognitive impairment may impair engagement with treatment (Level A), and cognitive screening should be performed for patients who have alcohol problems with referral for neuropsychological assessment if significant impairment is suspected (Level A)
claims.source_text: Cognitive impairment may impair engagement with treatment (Level A). Perform cognitive screening for patients who have alcohol problems and refer them for neuropsychological assessment if significant impairment is suspected (Level A).

claims.claim: Management should empower family and close friends to reduce availability of alcohol and encourage clinical engagement, consider medicolegal and ethical obligations relating to driving assessments, child protection, welfare, guardianship and employment, provide thiamine supplements to prevent further central nervous system damage, attend to advanced liver disease and other organ damage, and avoid interactions between medications for alcohol use disorders and other medications such as paracetamol, benzodiazepines, anticoagulants and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs
claims.source_text: Empower family and close friends to reduce availability of alcohol and encourage clinical engagement. Consider medicolegal and ethical obligations such as issues relating to: driving assessments; child protection; welfare; guardianship; and employment. Address specific medical and psychiatric conditions by: providing thiamine supplements to prevent further central nervous system damage; attending to advanced liver disease and other organ damage; and avoiding interactions between medications for alcohol use disorders and other medications (eg, paracetamol, benzodiazepines, anticoagulants and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs).
